ruteni.t: Gallic people of the Rouergue whose land later produced the red samian pottery of La Graufesenque, sold across the Roman world.
ruteni.o: The Ruteni lived in the modern Aveyron, around Segodunum (Rodez). After 121 BCE part of their territory was annexed to the Roman Province, so that Caesar distinguishes the Ruteni provinciales from the independent Ruteni.
ruteni.r: They were clients of the Arverni. Their land held silver mines, and they struck their own coins.
ruteni.e: The independent Ruteni joined Vercingetorix in 52 BCE. Under Rome Segodunum became Rodez, and the workshops of La Graufesenque near Millau made millions of red-gloss pots exported as far as India. The medieval Rouergue kept their name.

republic-of-ragusa.t: Aristocratic merchant republic of Dubrovnik, which grew rich on Balkan and Mediterranean trade and kept its freedom for four and a half centuries.
republic-of-ragusa.o: Ragusa (Dubrovnik) had been a Byzantine and then Venetian-ruled commune. In 1358, under the Treaty of Zadar, Venice gave up Dalmatia to Louis I of Hungary, and Ragusa became a self-governing republic under loose Hungarian protection.
republic-of-ragusa.r: Power lay with the noble Great Council; a rector served a one-month term to prevent anyone gaining personal power. Ragusan merchants carried silver, lead and goods from the Kingdom of Bosnia and Serbian mines, and their fleet traded across the Mediterranean. The republic paid tribute to the Ottomans from 1458 and stayed neutral, banned the slave trade in 1416 and set up early quarantine. Writers such as Marin Držić and Ivan Gundulić made it a centre of Croatian literature.
republic-of-ragusa.e: A great earthquake in 1667 devastated the city, but the republic recovered. French troops occupied it in 1806, and Marshal Marmont abolished it in 1808; it passed to Austria in 1815 and is now part of Croatia.

realm-of-jovan-nenad.t: Brief Serbian realm in the southern Hungarian plain, created by the self-proclaimed tsar Jovan Nenad in the chaos after the battle of Mohács.
realm-of-jovan-nenad.o: After the Ottoman victory at Mohács in 1526, a Serbian adventurer known as Jovan Nenad, the Black Man, gathered an army of Serbian refugees and peasants in Bačka and Banat that may have numbered 15,000. He drove off Ottoman raiders, took control of the region and proclaimed himself tsar, setting up his court at Subotica.
realm-of-jovan-nenad.r: His realm was a military regime resting on his army, which lived from the land and from requisitions on Hungarian nobles. In the contest for the Hungarian throne Jovan Nenad first backed John Zápolya, then switched to Ferdinand of Habsburg. His claim to a Serbian imperial title and his origins remain obscure, and contemporary accounts are partisan.
realm-of-jovan-nenad.e: Zápolya's forces defeated Jovan Nenad in the summer of 1527, and he was killed soon afterwards near Szeged. His army dispersed and the region fell to the Ottomans within a few years. Serbian tradition remembers him as a forerunner of later Serbian autonomy in Vojvodina.

republic-of-liege.t: The short-lived revolutionary government of Liège, which drove out its prince-bishop in 1789 in a 'happy revolution' inspired by events in Paris.
republic-of-liege.o: Resentment against the authoritarian prince-bishop Constantin-François de Hoensbroeck had grown among Liège's burghers and Enlightenment-minded elites. On 18 August 1789, weeks after the fall of the Bastille, citizens seized the town hall and installed new mayors; the prince-bishop fled, and the Prince-Bishopric of Liège came under patriot control.
republic-of-liege.r: The patriots, led by Jacques-Joseph Fabry and Jean-Rémy de Chestret, governed through a revived city council and the estates, proclaimed the rights of citizens and sought support from Prussia, whose troops briefly occupied the city. The revolution was largely bloodless and called the 'happy revolution', though divisions grew between moderates and radicals.
republic-of-liege.e: After Prussia withdrew, Austrian troops of the Holy Roman Empire restored the prince-bishop in January 1791. His return was brief: French armies arrived in 1792 and again in 1794, and Liège was annexed to France in 1795.

ringerike.t: Inland petty kingdom north-west of Oslo whose last king, Sigurd Syr, was stepfather of Saint Olaf and father of Harald Hardrada.
ringerike.o: Ringerike lay around Lake Tyrifjorden in the inland Upplands of eastern Norway. The sagas name a king Sigurd Hart as ruler here in the 9th century and make his daughter the mother of Harald Fairhair. Like its neighbours, it was a farming district ruled by local kings who might accept a more powerful overlord.
ringerike.r: The area was fertile and well settled, and its kings held large estates. Ringerike lent its name to an art style of the early 11th century, seen on carved stones quarried in the district, with tendrils and animal motifs. Local kings kept their titles under the overlordship of Harald Fairhair's successors.
ringerike.e: Its best-known king, Sigurd Syr, married Åsta, mother of Olaf Haraldsson, and supported Olaf's bid for the Norwegian throne in 1015. Sigurd died around 1018, and Olaf soon put an end to the Uppland petty kings, so Ringerike became part of the Kingdom of Norway. Sigurd's son was Harald Hardrada.

republic-of-crema.t: A brief Jacobin republic proclaimed in Crema in March 1797, when the town broke from Venice in the last weeks of the Serenissima.
republic-of-crema.o: Crema, a Lombard town between Milan and Cremona, had belonged to the Republic of Venice since 1449. On 28 March 1797, following the revolts of Bergamo and Brescia and with French troops present, local patriots deposed the Venetian governor and proclaimed the Cremasque Republic.
republic-of-crema.r: The republic was a provisional government of local notables and Jacobins under French protection. It abolished Venetian institutions and noble privileges, set up committees on the French model and looked to union with the new Lombard republics. Little is known of its brief administration.
republic-of-crema.e: After the fall of Venice in May 1797, Crema was absorbed into the Cisalpine Republic later that year, ending its separate existence.

regional-defence-council-of-aragon.t: An anarchist-led regional government in eastern Aragon during the Spanish Civil War, known for its sweeping rural collectives.
regional-defence-council-of-aragon.o: In the summer of 1936 anarchist militia columns from Catalonia advanced into eastern Aragon, where collectives sprang up in hundreds of villages. In October 1936 the CNT created the Regional Defence Council of Aragon, first at Fraga and then at Caspe, under Joaquín Ascaso.
regional-defence-council-of-aragon.r: The council organised the collectivisation of land and trade, in some villages abolishing money, and coordinated supplies for the Aragon front. It was later broadened to include other Republican parties and was recognised by Largo Caballero's government in December 1936, though Communists and Republicans criticised it.
regional-defence-council-of-aragon.e: After the May Days of 1937 weakened the anarchists, the Negrín government dissolved the council in August 1937. Enrique Líster's troops arrested its leaders and broke up many collectives. Aragon was overrun by Franco in 1938.

republic-of-estonia.t: The Estonian nation-state, declared in 1918, occupied by the Soviet Union from 1940 and restored in 1991 as a digital-minded EU and NATO member.
republic-of-estonia.o: The Salvation Committee declared the Republic of Estonia on 24 February 1918, building on the Autonomous Governorate of Estonia. After German occupation, Estonia fought the War of Independence against Soviet Russia and the Baltic German Landeswehr, and the Treaty of Tartu in February 1920 secured its independence.
republic-of-estonia.r: The interwar republic carried out a radical land reform breaking the Baltic German estates, and granted cultural autonomy to minorities. Konstantin Päts ruled by decree from 1934. The Soviet Union occupied Estonia in 1940, creating the Estonian Soviet Socialist Republic, followed by German occupation and renewed Soviet rule, with mass deportations.
republic-of-estonia.e: The Singing Revolution of the late 1980s led to the restoration of independence on 20 August 1991, based on legal continuity with the pre-war republic. Estonia joined the EU and NATO in 2004 and the eurozone in 2011, and became known for its e-government and technology sector.

roman-republic-1849.t: The republic proclaimed in Rome in 1849 and led by Mazzini, whose defence by Garibaldi against French troops became a legend of Italian unification.
roman-republic-1849.o: After the murder of Pope Pius IX's minister Pellegrino Rossi in November 1848, the pope fled to Gaeta in the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies. An elected Constituent Assembly met in Rome and on 9 February 1849 abolished the temporal power of the Papal States and proclaimed a republic.
roman-republic-1849.r: A triumvirate of Giuseppe Mazzini, Aurelio Saffi and Carlo Armellini governed. The republic abolished the death penalty, introduced religious freedom and drafted a democratic constitution, promulgated on 3 July 1849. Giuseppe Garibaldi led volunteers in defence of the city, notably on the Janiculum hill.
roman-republic-1849.e: Louis-Napoleon's France sent an army under General Oudinot, which besieged Rome from June and entered the city in early July 1849. Garibaldi retreated with his volunteers, and papal rule was restored under French protection.

republic-of-north-ingria.t: Breakaway state of the Ingrian Finns near Petrograd in 1919-1920, backed by Finland and returned to Soviet Russia by the Treaty of Tartu.
republic-of-north-ingria.o: The Ingrian Finns, Lutheran Finnish-speakers living around Petrograd, resisted Bolshevik requisitions and conscription. In 1919, with help from Finland, inhabitants of the northern Ingrian parishes near the Finnish border rose in revolt and declared the Republic of North Ingria, based in the village of Kirjasalo.
republic-of-north-ingria.r: The small republic had its own government, flag, stamps and an armed force of a few hundred men, and sought union with Finland. It controlled only a narrow strip of territory and depended on Finnish supplies and volunteers.
republic-of-north-ingria.e: In the Treaty of Tartu between Finland and Soviet Russia in October 1920, Finland agreed to return North Ingria, while Russia promised the Ingrians cultural autonomy. The republic was dissolved in December 1920, and many inhabitants fled to Finland. The promised autonomy was later revoked, and Ingrian Finns suffered Stalinist deportations.

republic-of-german-austria.t: The short-lived first Austrian republic of 1918-19, created from the German-speaking lands of the Habsburg monarchy and seeking union with Germany.
republic-of-german-austria.o: As Austria-Hungary dissolved, the German-speaking members of the Imperial Council formed a provisional national assembly on 21 October 1918. On 12 November 1918, the day after Emperor Charles I withdrew from government, it proclaimed the Republic of German-Austria, declaring it part of the German Republic.
republic-of-german-austria.r: Karl Renner of the Social Democrats led the government as state chancellor. The republic claimed the Sudetenland, South Tyrol and other German-speaking areas, but could not enforce these claims. It faced hunger, inflation, returning soldiers and a communist putsch attempt, and abolished the nobility and banished the Habsburgs in April 1919.
republic-of-german-austria.e: The Treaty of Saint-Germain in September 1919 forbade union with Germany and set Austria's borders. On 21 October 1919 the state was renamed the Republic of Austria, the First Austrian Republic.

republic-of-san-marino.t: Tiny republic on Monte Titano that claims to be the oldest surviving sovereign state and republic in the world, traditionally founded in 301.
republic-of-san-marino.o: Tradition holds that Saint Marinus, a Christian stonemason from the island of Rab in Dalmatia, founded a monastic community on Monte Titano on 3 September 301 to escape persecution under Diocletian. A self-governing community around the monastery and fortress is documented from the early Middle Ages, with an assembly of household heads, the Arengo.
republic-of-san-marino.r: San Marino has been governed since at least the 13th century by two Captains Regent elected every six months, with a Great and General Council as legislature. Its statutes of 1600 served as a written constitution. It kept its independence through its mountain position, alliances with the Montefeltro and recognition by the Papacy in 1631. Catholicism and Italian are dominant; the economy today rests on tourism, banking and stamps.
republic-of-san-marino.e: San Marino survived the occupation by Cardinal Alberoni in 1739–40, declined Napoleon's offer of more territory in 1797, sheltered Garibaldi in 1849 and was left independent at Italian unification. It joined the Council of Europe in 1988 and the United Nations in 1992.

republic-of-sassari.t: A self-governing Sardinian city-republic that rose from the ruins of the Judicate of Logudoro and wrote its laws partly in Sardinian.
republic-of-sassari.o: After the death of Adelasia ended the Judicate of Logudoro in 1259, the growing town of Sassari took control of its own affairs and part of the surrounding territory. From 1272 it governed itself as a commune under Pisan influence, before allying with the Republic of Genoa in 1294.
republic-of-sassari.r: The free commune was led by a podestà sent from Genoa and local councils. Its statutes of 1316, the Statuti Sassaresi, survive in Latin and Sardinian versions and regulated trade, farming and justice. Sassari lived from grain, livestock and trade through Porto Torres.
republic-of-sassari.e: In 1323 Sassari submitted to the Infante Alfonso of the Kingdom of Aragon at the start of the Aragonese conquest, becoming part of the new Kingdom of Sardinia. It revolted several times in the following years.

republic-of-ararat.t: A Kurdish self-proclaimed republic around Mount Ararat, crushed by Turkey in 1930.
republic-of-ararat.o: After the failure of the Sheikh Said rebellion of 1925, Kurdish nationalists founded the Xoybun league in 1927. That year, in October, it proclaimed a Kurdish republic in the region of Mount Ararat, near the borders with Iran and the Soviet Union, with Ihsan Nuri Pasha as military commander and the tribal leader Ibrahim Heski as civil governor.
republic-of-ararat.r: The republic was a rebel administration based in the mountain villages, with its centre at Kurd Ava, relying on tribal fighters and support from Kurdish exiles. Its control was limited to the Ararat massif and surrounding valleys.
republic-of-ararat.e: Turkey launched major campaigns in 1930, accompanied by mass killings in the Zilan valley. Using Iranian territory with Tehran's consent, Turkish forces encircled the rebels, who were defeated by autumn 1930. Turkey and Iran adjusted their border in 1932, giving Turkey the slopes of Little Ararat.

royal-prussia.t: The western part of Prussia that rebelled against the Teutonic Knights and lived for three centuries under the Polish Crown, keeping its own diet and privileges.
royal-prussia.o: In 1454 the towns and nobles of the Prussian Confederation rose against the State of the Teutonic Order and placed themselves under King Casimir IV of Poland. After the Thirteen Years' War, the Second Peace of Thorn in 1466 gave Poland Pomerelia, Chelmno Land, Malbork, Elblag and the Prince-Bishopric of Warmia, which together formed Royal Prussia.
royal-prussia.r: Royal Prussia kept wide autonomy, with its own diet, council and laws, and its great cities of Gdansk, Torun and Elblag were largely German-speaking and Lutheran after the Reformation. Gdansk shipped Polish grain to Amsterdam and became the Commonwealth's richest city. Nicolaus Copernicus was born in Torun in 1473. After the Union of Lublin in 1569 the province was drawn more closely into the Crown.
royal-prussia.e: The First Partition of Poland in 1772 gave most of Royal Prussia to the Kingdom of Prussia, which made it the province of West Prussia, and Gdansk and Torun followed in 1793. Gdansk later became the Free City of Danzig (1807-1814).

republic-of-saint-titus.t: Rebel republic proclaimed by Venetian colonists in Crete in 1363, which briefly united Latin and Greek Cretans against Venice.
republic-of-saint-titus.o: In 1363 Venice demanded a new tax from the feudal settlers of Venetian Crete to pay for repairs to the harbour of Candia. The colonists, already resentful at being excluded from power in Venice, rebelled under leaders including Marco Gradenigo and Tito Venier, imprisoned the Venetian duke and proclaimed independence under Saint Titus, patron of Crete.
republic-of-saint-titus.r: The rebels formed a government in Candia led by a governor and councillors. To win Greek support they made concessions to the Orthodox church and drew in Greek nobles such as the Kallergis family. Their republic lacked outside allies: the pope and other powers backed Venice.
republic-of-saint-titus.e: Venice sent a mercenary army under Luchino dal Verme, which retook Candia in May 1364. Leaders were executed and Saint Mark's banner restored, though Greek rebels led by the Kallergis brothers fought on until 1367.
